claim: Certain serine codons (the four TCN codons) in the gene for the biofilm repressor SinR caused a lowering of SinR levels under biofilm-inducing conditions.
source: Certain serine codons, the four TCN codons, in the gene for the biofilm repressor SinR caused a lowering of SinR levels under biofilm-inducing conditions.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing differential SinR protein levels among synonymous variants (Figure 1D,E) and ribosome profiling data showing increased ribosome density at UCN codons during biofilm formation (Figure 2B).

claim: Synonymous substitutions of TCN codons with AGC or AGT impaired biofilm formation and gene expression.
source: Synonymous substitutions of these TCN codons with AGC or AGT impaired biofilm formation and gene expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology assays (Figure 1C) showing flat, featureless colonies and β-galactosidase activity measurements (Figure 1G) showing reduced matrix gene expression.

claim: Switching AGC or AGT to TCN codons upregulated biofilm formation.
source: Conversely, switching AGC or AGT to TCN codons upregulated biofilm formation.
evidence: Supported by colony morphology data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing enhanced wrinkled appearance indicative of robust biofilm formation.

claim: Ribosome density was higher at UCN codons than at AGC or AGU during biofilm formation.
source: Genome-wide ribosome profiling showed that ribosome density was higher at UCN codons than at AGC or AGU during biofilm formation.
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling experiments showing that the four UCN codons had 1.9 to 2.1-fold higher ribosome density whereas the AGC and AGU codons had only 1.1 and 1.3-fold higher ribosome density respectively, relative to the median value across 61 sense codons (Figure 2B).

claim: Serine starvation recapitulated the effect of biofilm-inducing conditions on ribosome occupancy and SinR production.
source: Serine starvation recapitulated the effect of biofilm-inducing conditions on ribosome occupancy and SinR production.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data showing increased ribosome density at serine codons during serine starvation (Figure 3C) and differential SinR-YFP protein levels among synonymous variants during serine starvation (Figure 3A,B).

claim: Serine is one of the first amino acids to be exhausted at the end of exponential phase growth.
source: As serine is one of the first amino acids to be exhausted at the end of exponential phase growth, reduced translation speed at serine codons may be exploited by other microbes in adapting to stationary phase.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing serine depletion in B. subtilis and E. coli (Liebs et al., 1988; Prüss et al., 1994; Sezanov et al., 2007).

claim: The serine sensing mechanism operates without the involvement of a dedicated RNA or protein.
source: We report the discovery of a simple environmental sensing mechanism for biofilm formation in the bacterium Bacillus subtilis that operates without the involvement of a dedicated RNA or protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that synonymous codon changes alone are sufficient to alter biofilm formation without requiring additional regulatory factors.

claim: Biofilm formation in B. subtilis involves a switch from planktonic growth to the formation of complex, multicellular communities in response to environmental cues.
source: Biofilm formation involves a switch from planktonic growth as individual cells to the formation of complex, multicellular communities in response to environmental cues (Kolter and Greenberg, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on biofilm formation.

claim: In B. subtilis, biofilm communities are embedded in a self-produced matrix consisting of polysaccharide and an amyloid-like protein.
source: In B. subtilis, these communities are embedded in a self-produced matrix consisting of polysaccharide and an amyloid-like protein, which are specified by the epsA-O and the tapA-sipW-tasA operons, respectively (Branda et al., 2001; Kearns et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing the biofilm matrix components.

claim: The transition to multicellularity is governed in part by four histidine kinases (KinA, KinB, KinC and KinD) that control the phosphorylation of the response regulator Spo0A.
source: The transition to multicellularity is governed in part by four histidine kinases (KinA, KinB, KinC and KinD) that control the phosphorylation of the response regulator, Spo0A, a master regulator of post-exponential phase gene expression (Figure 1A) (Jiang et al., 2000; Vlamakis et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the regulatory circuit.

claim: KinA and KinB respond to impaired respiration.
source: Recent studies suggest that KinA and KinB respond to impaired respiration (Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2013), whereas KinC responds to membrane perturbations and KinD to unknown chemical signals (López et al., 2009; Shemesh et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012; Beauregard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent study on histidine kinase signaling.

claim: KinC responds to membrane perturbations.
source: Recent studies suggest that KinA and KinB respond to impaired respiration (Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2013), whereas KinC responds to membrane perturbations and KinD to unknown chemical signals (López et al., 2009; Shemesh et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012; Beauregard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on KinC signaling.

claim: KinD responds to unknown chemical signals.
source: Recent studies suggest that KinA and KinB respond to impaired respiration (Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2013), whereas KinC responds to membrane perturbations and KinD to unknown chemical signals (López et al., 2009; Shemesh et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012; Beauregard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies, though the specific signals remain unidentified.

claim: Once phosphorylated, Spo0A turns on sinI, a gene encoding a small protein antagonist of the biofilm-specific regulatory protein SinR.
source: Once phosphorylated, Spo0A turns on sinI, a gene encoding a small protein antagonist of the biofilm-specific regulatory protein SinR (Molle et al., 2003; Kearns et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing the Spo0A-SinI-SinR regulatory pathway.

claim: SinR is produced constitutively.
source: SinR, which is produced constitutively, is a repressor of the matrix operons, epsA-O and the tapA-sipW-tasA, as well as other biofilm-related genes (Kearns et al., 2005; Chu et al., 2006; Chai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on SinR regulation.

claim: SinR is a repressor of the matrix operons epsA-O and tapA-sipW-tasA, as well as other biofilm-related genes.
source: SinR, which is produced constitutively, is a repressor of the matrix operons, epsA-O and the tapA-sipW-tasA, as well as other biofilm-related genes (Kearns et al., 2005; Chu et al., 2006; Chai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing SinR's repressor function.

claim: SinR is also a repressor of the gene for SlrR.
source: SinR is also a repressor of the gene for SlrR (Chu et al., 2008), which together with SinR sets up a self-reinforcing, double-negative feedback loop for matrix gene expression (Figure 1A) (Chai et al., 2010; Norman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: SinR and SlrR set up a self-reinforcing, double-negative feedback loop for matrix gene expression.
source: SinR is also a repressor of the gene for SlrR (Chu et al., 2008), which together with SinR sets up a self-reinforcing, double-negative feedback loop for matrix gene expression (Figure 1A) (Chai et al., 2010; Norman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the regulatory circuit.

claim: The expression of matrix genes is hypersensitive to small perturbations in the level of SinR protein.
source: A special feature of SinR of relevance to this investigation is that the expression of matrix genes is hypersensitive to small perturbations in the level of the protein (Chai et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study demonstrating ultrasensitivity of matrix gene expression to SinR levels.

claim: The hypersensitivity of matrix gene expression to SinR levels is attributed to molecular titration of SinR by SinI and cooperativity among SinR molecules bound to tandem target sequences at regulatory sites for the matrix operons.
source: This hypersensitivity is attributed to molecular titration of SinR by SinI and cooperativity among SinR molecules bound to tandem target sequences at regulatory sites for the matrix operons (Chai et al., 2011; Chai et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing the molecular mechanisms underlying ultrasensitivity.

claim: The sinR coding sequence has a slightly higher frequency of the four TCN serine codons compared to the average frequency of TCN codons in the B. subtilis genome.
source: We noticed that the sinR coding sequence has a slightly higher frequency of the four TCN serine codons as compared to the average frequency of TCN codons in the B. subtilis genome (Figure 1B, p=0.22, N = 12).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of codon usage shown in Figure 1B, though the p-value indicates this difference is not statistically significant.

claim: Replacing the TCA codons in sinR with AGT or AGC resulted in flat, featureless colonies on solid biofilm-inducing medium, indicating severely impaired biofilm formation.
source: Replacing the TCA codons with AGT or AGC resulted in flat, featureless colonies on solid biofilm-inducing medium, indicating severely impaired biofilm formation (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Replacing the TCA codons in sinR with TCC or TCT had little or no effect on colony morphology.
source: In contrast, replacing the TCA codons with either TCC or TCT had little or no effect on colony morphology whereas switching to TCG increased the wrinkled appearance of the colonies (Figure 1C), which is indicative of robust biofilm formation.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Switching TCA codons in sinR to TCG increased the wrinkled appearance of the colonies, which is indicative of robust biofilm formation.
source: In contrast, replacing the TCA codons with either TCC or TCT had little or no effect on colony morphology whereas switching to TCG increased the wrinkled appearance of the colonies (Figure 1C), which is indicative of robust biofilm formation.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The strain with the AGT variant of sinR had slightly yet consistently higher SinR levels compared to either the wild-type strain with three TCA codons or the TCG variant of sinR.
source: Immunoblot analysis with anti-SinR antibodies revealed slightly yet consistently higher SinR levels in the strain with the AGT variant of sinR when compared to either the wild-type strain with three TCA codons or the TCG variant of sinR (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis and densitometry shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: SinR is highly similar (85% identity) to SlrR.
source: SinR is highly similar (85% identity) to SlrR, which also plays a critical role in biofilm formation and whose gene (slrR) is under the direct negative control of SinR (Chu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study characterizing the relationship between SinR and SlrR.

claim: SlrR plays a critical role in biofilm formation.
source: SinR is highly similar (85% identity) to SlrR, which also plays a critical role in biofilm formation and whose gene (slrR) is under the direct negative control of SinR (Chu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on SlrR function.

claim: The slrR gene is under the direct negative control of SinR.
source: SinR is highly similar (85% identity) to SlrR, which also plays a critical role in biofilm formation and whose gene (slrR) is under the direct negative control of SinR (Chu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on SinR-SlrR regulation.

claim: The levels of SlrR were almost perfectly anti-correlated with those of SinR among sinR synonymous variants.
source: Strikingly, the levels of SlrR were almost perfectly anti-correlated with those of SinR, with the differences in the SlrR protein levels among the sinR synonymous variants being much higher than the corresponding differences in SinR protein levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis and densitometry shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The differences in SlrR protein levels among the sinR synonymous variants were much higher than the corresponding differences in SinR protein levels.
source: Strikingly, the levels of SlrR were almost perfectly anti-correlated with those of SinR, with the differences in the SlrR protein levels among the sinR synonymous variants being much higher than the corresponding differences in SinR protein levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis and densitometry shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Repression by SinR is ultrasensitive to SinR levels.
source: Because repression by SinR is ultrasensitive to SinR levels (Chai et al., 2011), small differences in SinR protein levels among sinR synonymous variants might be sufficient to cause large differences in the levels of expression of SinR-repressed genes such as slrR.
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study demonstrating ultrasensitivity.

claim: Small differences in SinR protein levels among sinR synonymous variants might be sufficient to cause large differences in the levels of expression of SinR-repressed genes such as slrR.
source: Because repression by SinR is ultrasensitive to SinR levels (Chai et al., 2011), small differences in SinR protein levels among sinR synonymous variants might be sufficient to cause large differences in the levels of expression of SinR-repressed genes such as slrR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known ultrasensitivity of SinR repression and the observed differences in SlrR levels.

claim: The four TCN sinR variants had 3- to 19-fold higher β-galactosidase activity than the AGT and AGC variants.
source: Consistent with this idea, an eps-lacZ transcriptional fusion reporter for the SinR-repressed epsA-O matrix operon showed that the four TCN sinR variants had 3- to 19-fold higher β-galactosidase activity than the AGT and AGC variants (Figure 1G).
evidence: Demonstrated by β-galactosidase activity measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Eight out of eleven additional sinR synonymous variants conformed to the hierarchy where the four TCN variants behaved oppositely to the two AGC/AGT variants in colony morphology and eps-lacZ reporter expression.
source: Eight of these variants conformed to the hierarchy described above, namely, the four TCN variants behaved oppositely to the two AGC/AGT variants in colony morphology and in eps-lacZ reporter expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology and β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Three sinR synonymous variants did not conform to the hierarchy between TCN and AGC/AGT codons.
source: The three variants that did not conform to the hierarchy could potentially reflect alterations to the mRNA sequence context near the mutation rather than the effect of a synonymous substitution per se.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that not all variants followed the expected pattern.

claim: Serine synonymous codons in the sinR coding sequence have a stereotypical effect on biofilm formation that is primarily determined by the differential usage of the four TCN and the two AGC/AGT codons.
source: Taken together, the above results suggest that serine synonymous codons in the sinR coding sequence have a stereotypical effect on biofilm formation that is primarily determined by the differential usage of the four TCN and the two AGC/AGT codons.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the collective data on synonymous variants showing consistent patterns based on codon type.

claim: Synonymous codon changes can alter the synthesis of the encoded protein through changes in the translation initiation rate, mRNA levels or the ribosome elongation rate.
source: Synonymous codon changes can alter the synthesis of the encoded protein through changes in the translation initiation rate, mRNA levels or the ribosome elongation rate (Plotkin and Kudla, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review on synonymous codon effects.

claim: The effect of synonymous codon usage on the initiation rate and mRNA levels is context-specific.
source: However, the effect of synonymous codon usage on the initiation rate and mRNA levels is context-specific; only codons near the AUG start site affect translation initiation (Kudla et al., 2009), whereas only codons that are located in certain regions of secondary structure or at ribonuclease cleavage sites affect mRNA levels (Bernstein et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on context-specific effects of synonymous codons.

claim: Only codons near the AUG start site affect translation initiation.
source: However, the effect of synonymous codon usage on the initiation rate and mRNA levels is context-specific; only codons near the AUG start site affect translation initiation (Kudla et al., 2009), whereas only codons that are located in certain regions of secondary structure or at ribonuclease cleavage sites affect mRNA levels (Bernstein et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on translation initiation.

claim: Only codons that are located in certain regions of secondary structure or at ribonuclease cleavage sites affect mRNA levels.
source: However, the effect of synonymous codon usage on the initiation rate and mRNA levels is context-specific; only codons near the AUG start site affect translation initiation (Kudla et al., 2009), whereas only codons that are located in certain regions of secondary structure or at ribonuclease cleavage sites affect mRNA levels (Bernstein et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on mRNA stability.

claim: Synonymous codon replacements at multiple locations along sinR have a stereotypical effect on biofilm formation, arguing against context-specific mechanisms.
source: Our observation that synonymous codon replacements at multiple locations along sinR have a stereotypical effect on biofilm formation argues against such context-specific mechanisms (except for the three exceptional cases noted above).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutations at different positions have similar effects.

claim: The ribosome elongation rate at a codon varies inversely with the average ribosome density at that codon.
source: To test the alternative hypothesis that serine codon usage might alter the ribosome elongation rate, and given that the ribosome elongation rate at a codon varies inversely with the average ribosome density at that codon, we measured ribosome density on mRNAs at single-codon resolution using the ribosome profiling method (Ingolia et al., 2009; Oh et al., 2011; Ingolia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between ribosome density and elongation rate, supported by citations to ribosome profiling methodology papers.

claim: Ribosome profiling yielded 3.75 and 2.55 million sequencing reads aligning to annotated protein-coding sequences for the exponential phase sample and the biofilm entry sample, respectively.
source: Ribosome profiling yielded 3.75 and 2.55 million sequencing reads aligning to annotated protein-coding sequences for the exponential phase sample and the biofilm entry sample, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of the sequencing data obtained from the ribosome profiling experiments.

claim: The number of reads aligning to a single codon on individual mRNAs was too low for accurate quantification of ribosome density.
source: The number of reads aligning to a single codon on individual mRNAs was too low for accurate quantification of ribosome density, and was not sufficient to directly detect increased ribosome density on the sinR transcript.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a technical limitation in the ribosome profiling data.

claim: The global pattern of ribosome density at codons across all mRNAs should reflect the ribosome density on individual transcripts such as sinR.
source: However, we reasoned that the global pattern of ribosome density at codons across all mRNAs should reflect the ribosome density on individual transcripts such as sinR.
evidence: This is a logical inference used to justify the genome-wide analysis approach.

claim: The ribosome profiling analysis reproduced the previous observation of increased ribosome density 8 to 11 nt downstream of Shine-Dalgarno-like trinucleotide sequences.
source: This analysis reproduced the previous observation (Li et al., 2012) of increased ribosome density 8 to 11 nt downstream of Shine-Dalgarno-like trinucleotide sequences both during exponential phase and during biofilm entry (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This serves as a validation of the ribosome profiling methodology by reproducing a known result, supported by citation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: During exponential phase, median ribosome density varied over a twofold range, with no systematic difference between serine codons and the remaining codons.
source: During exponential phase, median ribosome density varied over a twofold range, with no systematic difference between serine codons and the remaining codons (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: During biofilm entry, median ribosome density was significantly higher at serine and cysteine codons as compared to the remaining codons.
source: By contrast, during biofilm entry, median ribosome density was significantly higher at serine and cysteine codons as compared to the remaining codons (Figure 2B), suggesting that the translation speed of ribosomes is selectively reduced at these codons during biofilm entry.
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The translation speed of ribosomes is selectively reduced at serine and cysteine codons during biofilm entry.
source: By contrast, during biofilm entry, median ribosome density was significantly higher at serine and cysteine codons as compared to the remaining codons (Figure 2B), suggesting that the translation speed of ribosomes is selectively reduced at these codons during biofilm entry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased ribosome density at these codons, given the inverse relationship between ribosome density and elongation rate.

claim: The ribosome density at serine codons was not uniform during biofilm entry.
source: Notably, the ribosome density at serine codons was not uniform: the four UCN codons had 1.9 to 2.1-fold higher ribosome density whereas the AGC and AGU codons had only 1.1 and 1.3-fold higher ribosome density respectively, relative to the median value across 61 sense codons.
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data analysis.

claim: The difference in ribosome density between UCN codons and the AGC/AGU codons was essentially identical when computed separately for codons located in the first half or in the second half of each gene.
source: Further, this difference in ribosome density between UCN codons and the AGC/AGU codons was essentially identical when computed separately for codons located in the first half or in the second half of each gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), a finding that underscores the statistical robustness and the context independence of the observed difference.
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The increased ribosome density at serine and cysteine codons during biofilm entry was caused by the depletion of intracellular pools of these two amino acids rather than by any intrinsic feature of the mRNA or the nascent polypeptide.
source: Because ribosomes density increased at serine and cysteine codons only during biofilm formation and not during exponential phase growth, we hypothesized that the increased ribosome density was caused by the depletion of intracellular pools of these two amino acids during biofilm entry rather than by any intrinsic feature of the mRNA (Li et al., 2012) or the nascent polypeptide (Charneski and Hurst, 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the condition-specific nature of the increased ribosome density, supported by citations to alternative mechanisms.

claim: Synonymous codon usage can have a starvation-specific effect on protein levels.
source: Our hypothesis is also supported by the previous observation that synonymous codon usage can have a starvation-specific effect on protein levels (Subramaniam et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on codon usage effects during starvation.

claim: Serine is a precursor metabolite for the biosynthesis of cysteine.
source: Further, serine is a precursor metabolite for the biosynthesis of cysteine (Gagnon et al., 1994); hence cysteine depletion was likely the result of a decrease in intracellular serine concentration.
evidence: Supported by citation to a study on amino acid biosynthesis pathways.

claim: Cysteine depletion was likely the result of a decrease in intracellular serine concentration.
source: Further, serine is a precursor metabolite for the biosynthesis of cysteine (Gagnon et al., 1994); hence cysteine depletion was likely the result of a decrease in intracellular serine concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biosynthetic relationship between serine and cysteine.

claim: Serine starvation resulted in an increase in ribosome density at both serine and cysteine codons.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we also observed an increase in ribosome density at both serine and cysteine codons during serine starvation of a B. subtilis serine-auxotrophic mutant (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data from serine starvation experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Serine starvation resulted in an increase in ribosome density at only the four UCN serine codons but not at the AGC and AGU codons.
source: Importantly, serine starvation resulted in an increase in ribosome density at only the four UCN serine codons but not at the AGC and AGU codons, matching the hierarchy seen during biofilm entry (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data from serine starvation experiments shown in Figure 3C, compared to biofilm entry data in Figure 2B.

claim: Serine starvation resulted in differential levels of production of SinR-YFP protein fusions bearing different synonymous serine codons.
source: Serine starvation also resulted in differential levels of production of SinR-YFP protein fusions bearing different synonymous serine codons, whereas serine-rich growth resulted in identical levels of fusion protein production from these variants (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by YFP fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Serine-rich growth resulted in identical levels of SinR-YFP fusion protein production from synonymous variants.
source: Serine starvation also resulted in differential levels of production of SinR-YFP protein fusions bearing different synonymous serine codons, whereas serine-rich growth resulted in identical levels of fusion protein production from these variants (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by YFP fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The addition of excess serine or cysteine (but not any of the other 18 amino acids) blocked biofilm formation in wild type cells.
source: Finally, the addition of excess serine or cysteine (but not any of the other 18 amino acids) blocked biofilm formation in wild type cells as judged after 48 hr of growth in biofilm-inducing medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by pellicle formation assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fold-change in average ribosome density of B. subtilis genes was positively correlated between biofilm entry and serine starvation.
source: The fold-change in average ribosome density of B. subtilis genes was positively correlated between biofilm entry and serine starvation (Figure 3D, R2 = 0.27, p=10−5, 1724 genes).
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis of ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A subset of 68 genes was induced at least 10-fold higher upon biofilm entry than during serine starvation.
source: However, a subset of 68 genes was induced at least 10-fold higher upon biofilm entry than during serine starvation (indicated by red markers in Figure 3D, Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data analysis shown in Figure 3D and listed in Table 1.

claim: The subset of genes preferentially induced during biofilm entry included genes for anaerobic metabolism such as lctEP, nasDE, and cydAB.
source: This subset included genes for anaerobic metabolism such as lctEP, nasDE, and cydAB, and is consistent with the recently proposed role of impaired respiration in biofilm formation (Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by gene ontology analysis of the differentially expressed genes, supported by citation to a study on respiration and biofilm formation.

claim: Sulfur metabolism genes were enriched in the subset of genes preferentially induced during biofilm entry.
source: We observed that sulfur metabolism genes were also enriched in this subset, possibly indicating a stronger response to cysteine depletion during biofilm entry than during serine starvation.
evidence: This is an observation from gene ontology analysis with a speculative interpretation.

claim: UCN codons lower SinR levels by slowing the rate of ribosome movement along the mRNA (elongation).
source: We presume that UCN codons lower SinR levels simply by slowing the rate of ribosome movement along the mRNA (elongation).
evidence: This is a presumption based on the observed increase in ribosome density at UCN codons.

claim: The reduced translation speed at UCN codons during biofilm entry could be followed by downstream events such as ribosome rescue or mRNA decay that might also contribute to lowering the levels of the SinR protein.
source: However, it is possible that the reduced translation speed at UCN codons during biofilm entry could be followed by downstream events such as ribosome rescue (Keiler et al., 1996) or mRNA decay (Hayes and Sauer, 2003) that might also contribute to lowering the levels of the SinR protein.
evidence: This is a speculation about possible additional mechanisms, supported by citations to studies on ribosome rescue and mRNA decay.

claim: The serine sensing mechanism operates through over-representation of the TCN serine codons in the sinR gene without the necessity for any other dedicated protein or RNA for sensing serine depletion.
source: The serine sensing mechanism uncovered here operates through over-representation of the TCN serine codons in the sinR gene without the necessity for any other dedicated protein or RNA for sensing serine depletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data showing that codon usage alone is sufficient for the sensing mechanism.

claim: Transcriptional attenuation is a widespread mechanism among bacteria for sensing amino acids that relies on changes in translation speed.
source: By contrast, transcriptional attenuation, a widespread mechanism among bacteria for sensing amino acids that also relies on changes in translation speed, involves a translation-transcription coupling mechanism that is mediated by highly structured mRNAs and leader peptides (Henkin and Yanofsky, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review on transcriptional attenuation mechanisms.

claim: Transcriptional attenuation involves a translation-transcription coupling mechanism that is mediated by highly structured mRNAs and leader peptides.
source: By contrast, transcriptional attenuation, a widespread mechanism among bacteria for sensing amino acids that also relies on changes in translation speed, involves a translation-transcription coupling mechanism that is mediated by highly structured mRNAs and leader peptides (Henkin and Yanofsky, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review on transcriptional attenuation mechanisms.

claim: The biased usage of the four TCN serine codons is not evident from widely-used phenomenological measures of codon bias such as the codon adaptation index.
source: We note that the biased usage of the four TCN serine codons, which act as starvation sensors during biofilm formation, is not evident from widely-used phenomenological measures of codon bias such as the codon adaptation index (Figure 4D), which primarily reflects codon preferences during exponential growth (Sharp and Li, 1987; Andersson and Kurland, 1990).
evidence: Demonstrated by CAI analysis shown in Figure 4D, supported by citations to studies on codon adaptation index.

claim: The codon adaptation index primarily reflects codon preferences during exponential growth.
source: We note that the biased usage of the four TCN serine codons, which act as starvation sensors during biofilm formation, is not evident from widely-used phenomenological measures of codon bias such as the codon adaptation index (Figure 4D), which primarily reflects codon preferences during exponential growth (Sharp and Li, 1987; Andersson and Kurland, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational studies on the codon adaptation index.

claim: The difference in translation speed between the four UCN codons and the two AGC/AGU codons under biofilm-inducing conditions is likely mediated by differences in concentration of the corresponding aminoacylated tRNAs.
source: The difference in translation speed between the four UCN codons and the two AGC/AGU codons under biofilm-inducing conditions is likely mediated by differences in concentration of the corresponding aminoacylated tRNAs (Elf et al., 2003; Dittmar et al., 2005), as was recently observed in serine-starved E. coli (Subramaniam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on established mechanisms of codon-specific translation speed, supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: The hierarchy between UCN codons and AGC/AGU codons in B. subtilis during serine starvation is similar to the one in E. coli.
source: Interestingly, the hierarchy between UCN codons and AGC/AGU codons in B. subtilis during serine starvation is similar to the one in E. coli even though copy numbers of the corresponding tRNA genes have diverged significantly between these two organisms (Lowe and Eddy, 1997).
evidence: This is an observation comparing the current findings to previous work in E. coli, supported by citation to a tRNA gene database.

claim: Copy numbers of serine tRNA genes have diverged significantly between B. subtilis and E. coli.
source: Interestingly, the hierarchy between UCN codons and AGC/AGU codons in B. subtilis during serine starvation is similar to the one in E. coli even though copy numbers of the corresponding tRNA genes have diverged significantly between these two organisms (Lowe and Eddy, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to a tRNA gene database study.

claim: It is possible that the relative abundances of the serine tRNA isoacceptors are similar between B. subtilis and E. coli despite different tRNA gene copy numbers.
source: Despite different tRNA gene copy numbers, it is possible that the relative abundances of the serine tRNA isoacceptors are similar between the two organisms or that their relative abundances might be regulated in the same manner in response to nutrient deprivation (Doi et al., 1966).
evidence: This is a speculation about possible explanations for the conserved hierarchy, supported by citation to a study on tRNA regulation.

claim: The relative abundances of serine tRNA isoacceptors might be regulated in the same manner in B. subtilis and E. coli in response to nutrient deprivation.
source: Despite different tRNA gene copy numbers, it is possible that the relative abundances of the serine tRNA isoacceptors are similar between the two organisms or that their relative abundances might be regulated in the same manner in response to nutrient deprivation (Doi et al., 1966).
evidence: This is a speculation about possible regulatory mechanisms, supported by citation to a study on tRNA regulation.

claim: Serine is one of the first amino acids to be completely consumed from the culture medium when either B. subtilis or E. coli cells are grown in complex rich medium.
source: Serine is one of the first amino acids to be completely consumed from the culture medium when either B. subtilis or E. coli cells are grown in complex rich medium (Liebs et al., 1988; Prüss et al., 1994; Sezanov et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies measuring amino acid consumption during bacterial growth.

claim: Increased ribosome density has been observed at serine codons during growth of E. coli in Luria-Bertani broth.
source: Indeed, increased ribosome density has been observed at serine codons during growth of E. coli in Luria-Bertani broth (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous ribosome profiling study in E. coli.

claim: The role of synonymous serine codons as starvation sensors discovered in the context of biofilm formation might be a general regulatory strategy in microbes for adapting to nutrient depletion at the end of exponential phase growth.
source: Thus the role of synonymous serine codons as starvation sensors discovered here in the specific context of biofilm formation might be a general regulatory strategy in microbes for adapting to nutrient depletion at the end of exponential phase growth.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader significance of the findings, based on the observation that serine is commonly depleted during stationary phase.

claim: Depletion of specific amino acids affects developmental transitions in several eukaryotic cells.
source: It is noteworthy that depletion of specific amino acids affects developmental transitions in several eukaryotic cells (Marin, 1976; Sundrud et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on amino acid sensing in eukaryotic development.

claim: It will be interesting to test whether a codon-based sensing mechanism, similar to the one found in bacterial biofilm development, also plays a role in eukaryotic cells during amino acid depletion.
source: It will be interesting to test whether a codon-based sensing mechanism, similar to the one found here in bacterial biofilm development, also plays a role in eukaryotic cells during amino acid depletion.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: A 3610-ΔepsH strain was used for ribosome profiling during biofilm formation to ensure dispersed growth in liquid media.
source: For ribosome profiling during biofilm formation, a 3610-ΔepsH strain (RL3852) was used to ensure dispersed growth in liquid media (Kearns et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citation to a previous study characterizing this strain.

claim: A serine-auxotrophic 3610-ΔserA strain was used for serine starvation experiments.
source: For serine starvation experiments, a serine-auxotrophic 3610-ΔserA strain (YC865) was used.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the strain used for specific experiments.

claim: The genetic screen recovered a variant that contained a silent mutation resulting in a switch from one serine codon to a synonymous codon in sinR.
source: In a genetic screen to identify suppressor mutations that rescued the biofilm-defective phenotype of a B. subtilis mutant ('Materials and methods'), we unexpectedly recovered a variant that contained a 'silent' mutation that resulted in a switch from one serine codon to a synonymous codon in sinR.
evidence: This is a description of the initial observation that led to the study.

claim: The four TCN codons are over-represented in two nucleotide biosynthesis genes, pyrAA and purB.
source: For example, we found that the four TCN codons are over-represented in two nucleotide biosynthesis genes, pyrAA and purB (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by codon usage analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The genes pyrAA and purB are transcriptionally down regulated during biofilm entry.
source: These two genes are also transcriptionally down regulated during biofilm entry (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data showing fold-change in expression shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A high frequency of TCN codons in pyrAA and purB might serve to reinforce their transcriptional down regulation by reducing translation speed.
source: A high frequency of TCN codons in these genes might serve to reinforce their transcriptional down regulation by reducing translation speed.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of codon usage in these genes.

claim: TCN codons are under-represented in the genes encoding lactate dehydrogenase (ldh) and a master regulator of post-exponential phase gene expression (spo0A).
source: Conversely, TCN codons are under-represented in the genes encoding lactate dehydrogenase, ldh (Cruz Ramos et al., 2000) and a master regulator of post-exponential phase gene expression, spo0A (Molle et al., 2003) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by codon usage analysis shown in Figure 4A, supported by citations to studies characterizing these genes.

claim: The genes ldh and spo0A are transcriptionally up regulated upon biofilm entry.
source: The two genes are transcriptionally up regulated upon biofilm entry (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data showing fold-change in expression shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The low frequency of TCN codons in ldh and spo0A might represent a mechanism for optimizing the production of their protein products by minimizing the slowing down of translation during biofilm entry.
source: The low frequency of TCN codons in these genes might represent a mechanism for optimizing the production of their protein products by minimizing the slowing down of translation during biofilm entry.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of codon usage in these genes.

claim: Replacement of AGC/AGT codons by TCN codons in spo0A resulted in defective biofilm formation.
source: Consistent with this idea, replacement of AGC/AGT codons by TCN codons in spo0A, whose protein product positively regulates biofilm entry (by turning on the synthesis of the SinR antagonist SinI), resulted in defective biofilm formation (Figure 4C) in contrast to the stimulatory effect of replacing AGC/AGT codons with TCN codons in sinR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony morphology assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Spo0A protein product positively regulates biofilm entry by turning on the synthesis of the SinR antagonist SinI.
source: Consistent with this idea, replacement of AGC/AGT codons by TCN codons in spo0A, whose protein product positively regulates biofilm entry (by turning on the synthesis of the SinR antagonist SinI), resulted in defective biofilm formation (Figure 4C) in contrast to the stimulatory effect of replacing AGC/AGT codons with TCN codons in sinR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Spo0A function in the biofilm regulatory circuit.

claim: Serine depletion is an environmental cue that contributes to promoting biofilm formation in B. subtilis together with other cues that are sensed by the histidine kinases KinA–D.
source: Together, our results implicate serine depletion as an environmental cue that contributes to promoting biofilm formation in B. subtilis together with other cues that are sensed by the histidine kinases KinA–D.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data showing that serine depletion affects biofilm formation.

claim: Serine depletion is sensed through a mechanism based on reduced translation speed at UCN serine codons in the mRNA for SinR.
source: Serine depletion is sensed through a remarkably simple mechanism based on reduced translation speed at UCN serine codons in the mRNA for a regulatory protein, SinR, whose repressive effects are highly sensitive to small changes in the level of the protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data on codon-specific ribosome density and SinR protein levels.

claim: The average ribosome density on any gene is directly proportional to the corresponding mRNA level in the absence of specific translational regulation.
source: We note that the average ribosome density on any gene is directly proportional to the corresponding mRNA level in the absence of specific translational regulation. Hence fold-changes in ribosome density (such as the one shown in Figure 3D) primarily reflect fold-changes in mRNA level.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the interpretation of ribosome profiling data.

claim: Fold-changes in ribosome density primarily reflect fold-changes in mRNA level.
source: We note that the average ribosome density on any gene is directly proportional to the corresponding mRNA level in the absence of specific translational regulation. Hence fold-changes in ribosome density (such as the one shown in Figure 3D) primarily reflect fold-changes in mRNA level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between ribosome density and mRNA levels.
